newsitem.title: UK: British film makers bemoan lottery cash share out.
newsitem.headline: British film makers bemoan lottery cash share out.

text.p: Movie makers who lost bids for funds from Britain's national lottery said on Friday they were shattered by the decision but held out hope more cash might eventually come their way.

The Arts Council of England shocked the industry on Thursday by allocating just over 90 million pounds ($150 million) of lottery funds to film groups out of the nearly 160 million pounds it had at its disposal.
The arts group awarded only three lottery franchises out of four that were available under its ambitious scheme to boost investment in Britain's film industry.

Among the 37 bidders for the funding, one of the most high-profile losers was a group formed by Merchant Ivory Productions, the force behind such British hits as "A Room With a View" and "Howard's End".
One of the winning franchises went to Pathe Productions , a group of British producers backed by French companies Pathe Pictures and Canal Plus, among others.
"It is a real slap in the face," said Premila Hoon of Guinness Mahon, the investment bank that formed part of Merchant Ivory's consortium.
Hoon was waiting at the Savoy Hotel in Cannes with producer Ismail Merchant and other members of the group on Thursday when she got news of the fund allocation.

"Although he was shattered by this, he said Onwards and upwards. We must keep this consortium together. We've got a superb business plan.' He put a very, very brave face on it," Hoon said in an interview.
Several film industry insiders said they held out hope that the Arts Council would award the rest of the money to film makers in the future.
"It would have been nice if all four franchises would have been invested, and we hope to see an additional franchise awarded," said Andrew Patrick, chief executive of the British Film Commission.
Arts Council officials could not be reached for comment on their plans for the rest of the lottery funds.

Besides Pathe, the winning groups were the Film Consortium, which included Richard Branson's Virgin Cinema, and DNA Film Ltd, formed by Andrew Macdonald, the producer of "Shallow Grave" and "Trainspotting".
Each group will receive some 30 million pounds of lottery funds over six years.
The consortia planned to produce more than 90 films, representing a total investment of over 460 million pounds in Britain's film industry.
Lottery funding will make up 20 to 35 percent of each film's budget with the groups left to find the remainder from the private sector.
"The sum is very significant because it's a multiplier," said Paul Styles, head of broadcasting consulting at KPMG, which advised the Film Consortium on its winning bid.
"You're looking at a pot of money that equates to a very significant boost to the industry," he added. ($1=.6098 Pound) ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
